questions.q: Per this lesson, what does Chainlink's own current documentation say about Automation and Functions?
options: Both have been deprecated, with guidance to migrate to the Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE)
Both are the current, actively recommended products for new integrations with no planned changes
Automation was deprecated but Functions remains the current recommendation
Both were merged into Chainlink Price Feeds and no longer exist as separate products
questions.explain: The lesson states this as a live finding checked directly against docs.chain.link: both products carry deprecation notices pointing builders to CRE.

questions.q: What specific gap did Chainlink Automation's checkUpkeep/performUpkeep pattern solve?
options: A smart contract can't wake itself up — something external needs to trigger performUpkeep when a condition is met
A smart contract can't read its own storage variables
A smart contract can't verify a signature without an oracle
A smart contract can't emit events without Automation installed
questions.explain: The lesson defines this directly: contracts are passive and need something external to call performUpkeep when a trigger condition is met.

questions.q: Why does performUpkeep re-check its own condition instead of just trusting that checkUpkeep already confirmed it should run?
options: Because checkUpkeep's result comes from an off-chain simulation, and chain state can shift between that check and performUpkeep's actual on-chain execution
Because checkUpkeep is not actually called by the Chainlink network at all
Because Solidity requires every external function to repeat its caller's validation logic by convention
It doesn't re-check — the lesson explains performUpkeep always trusts checkUpkeep's result unconditionally
questions.explain: The lesson explains this safety detail directly: checkUpkeep is an off-chain simulation, so performUpkeep must not blindly trust it given state can change before execution.

questions.q: What specific gap did Chainlink Functions solve, per this lesson?
options: Running off-chain computation or an authenticated API call that a contract itself can't make, with results aggregated across a decentralized oracle network
Giving contracts the ability to directly modify another contract's storage
Eliminating the need for gas fees on any transaction
Replacing Ethereum's consensus mechanism with a faster alternative
questions.explain: Functions is described as solving the problem of needing real computation or authenticated API access a contract can't do itself, using the same independent-nodes-plus-aggregation pattern as price feeds.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does the underlying pattern behind Automation and Functions still matter even though both products are deprecated?
options: The two problems they solved — triggering logic without a human, and bridging off-chain computation in safely — don't disappear; CRE addresses the same problems on the same underlying foundation
It doesn't matter at all; the lesson recommends skipping both patterns entirely going forward
Because Automation and Functions will un-deprecate once CRE is shut down
Because Solidity compilers still require AutomationCompatibleInterface to be imported in every contract
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is explicit: the specific interfaces change, but the underlying problems — and CRE's approach to them — remain the same independent-node, aggregated, incentive-backed shape from Lesson 17.
